III. אוֹן Gen. 41, 50 and אֹן 41, 45. 46,
20, On, the domestic pr. n. of an ancient
Egyptian city, in Ez. 30, 17 written אָוֶן
q. v. no. 1. b. Called also by the He-
brews, prob. as a translation of the
Egyptian name, בֵּית שֶׁמֶשׁ Beth-shemesh,
i. e. house of the sun, Jer. 43, 13; by
the Greeks Heliopolis, city of the sun;
by the Arabs عين شمس ’Ain Shems,
i. e. fountain of the sun. Coptic Ⲱⲛ,
which signified light, and spec. the sun,
as there seems hardly a doubt; comp.
ⲟⲩⲉⲓⲛ, ⲟⲉⲓⲛ, ⲟⲩⲱⲓⲛⲓ, light, lumi-
nary; see Peyron Lex. p. 273. The city
stood on the eastern side of the Nile, a
few miles north of Memphis; and was
celebrated for the worship and temple
of the sun, and for its obelisks, one of
which remains to the present day;
Diod. Sic. I. 85. Hdot. 2. 59. Near the
ruins of the ancient city is a fountain
still called 'Ain Shems, in the adjacent
modern village of Matarîyeh. Comp.
Descr. de l'Egypte, Antiq. V. Pl. 26, 27.
Bibl. Res. in Pal. I. p. 36, 37.
אוֹנוֹ (strong, for אוֹנוֹן) Ono, pr. n. of
a city in Benjamin, Ezra 2, 33. Neh. 7,
37. 11, 35. 1 Chr. 8, 12; with a valley
or plain of like name, Neh. 6, 2.
אוֹנִיּוֹת f. plur. 2 Chr. 8, 18 Cheth. for
אֳנִיּוֹת ships, with Vav as mater lectionis
redundant.
אוֹנָם (strong, stout) Onam, pr. n. m.
אוֹנָן (id.) Onan, pr. n. of a son of
אוּפָז Uphaz, pr. n. of a gold country,
Jer. 10, 9. Dan. 10, 5. It seems to be
corrupted out of אוֹפִּיר; since the letters
ר and ז are also elsewhere interchanged,
comp. בָּזָק and בָּרָק lightning, فخر and
فخز to boast.
אוֹפִיר, אוֹפִר, אֹפִיר, pr. n. Ophir,
a celebrated region, abounding in gold,
which the seamen of Solomon in com-
pany with the Phenicians were accus-
tomed to visit, taking their departure
from the ports of the Elanitic gulf, and
bringing back every three years gold,
precious stones, and sandal-wood, also
silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks; 1 K. 9,
10, 22, where Ophir is to be understood,
although not expressly mentioned. The
gold of Ophir is frequently mentioned
in the O. T. as Job 28, 16. Ps. 45, 10. Is.
13, 12. 1 Chr. 29, 4; once also אוֹפִיר
itself is put for gold of Ophir Job 22, 24.
As to the geographical situation of
Ophir, there is the greatest diversity
of opinion among commentators. Yet
among modern interpreters, the best
hesitate only between two regions, viz.
India, and some part of Arabia.—That
Ophir is to be sought in India, was the
opinion of Josephus (Ant. 8. 6. 4), and
among the moderns, of Vitringa, Reland,
and others; and this view is supported
by the following arguments: a) The
countries of India abound in the arti-
cles of traffic above mentioned; and se-
veral of these, as ivory and sandal-wood,
are found only in India; also the words
for apes and peacocks correspond en-
tirely with the Indian words for the same
on the coast of Malabar, and are doubt-
less derived from these latter; see קוֹף,
תֻּכִּיִּים. b) The LXX have everywhere
(except once in Gen. 10, 29) for אוֹפִיר
put Σουφίρ, Σουφείρ, Σωφίρ, Σωφείρ, Σω-
φαρά, Σωφηρά. But ⲥⲟϥⲓⲣ, according
to the ancient Coptic lexicographers,
(whose authority, however, is not very
great,) is the name for India. c) There
exists in India a district from the name
of which both the names Ophir and So-
phir may be readily explained, viz. Σου-
πάρα, the Οὔππαρα of Arrian, (Sanscr.
Uppara upper,) situated in the hither
Chersonesus where is now the celebrated
emporium of Goa, and mentioned by
Ptolemy, Ammianus, and Abulfeda.—
Of not less weight are the arguments
brought in favour of Arabia; which
view is supported among the moderns
by Michaelis (Spicil. II. p. 184 sq.) Gos-
selin, Vincent, Bredow (Histor. Unters.
II. p. 253), T. C. Tychsen, Seetzen in
Zach’s Monatl. Corresp. XIX. p. 331 sq.
and others. It is said: a) That Ophir,

line_status.note: The third letter of the right-hand word has a flat base that projects to the right beyond the upright stroke, and no inner curled lip — a bet, not a pe. Page 24 of Robinson's Gesenius begins with אוֹב and ends with אוֹן, matching the header. No vowel points are legible in the header at this enlargement.

The only difference is the mark before "Ain": the print shows a curved raised comma (’, the usual 19th-century rendering of ʿayin), not a straight typewriter apostrophe, so Reading B is correct. Arabic عين شمس (with shin dots) and the italic "Ain Shems," match in both.
The second Coptic letter is printed at x-height, clearly shorter than the capital Ⲱ before it, so it is lowercase ⲛ (Reading A), not capital Ⲛ (Reading B).

The vav dot is at mid-height inside the letter (shureq, אוּ), not above it as a holem — contrast the clearly raised holem on אוֹפִיר in line 3. The pe shows only qamets beneath, no dagesh. Reading A matches.
The pe in אוֹפִּיר shows a printed dot inside the letter (dagesh), in addition to the hireq beneath; the vav carries holem and the yod is plene. Reading A omits the dagesh.

Decisive difference is the left-to-right order of the three forms: printed leftmost is the fully plene אוֹפִיר, middle is אוֹפִר (no yod), rightmost is אֹפִיר (holem on alef, no vav) — Reading B's order; Reading A reversed it. Vowel points agree with both readings. The print has a visible space before each comma after the Hebrew, which only A reproduced.
